summary: This file converts MDX blog posts (which contain React components and JSX) into plain Markdown by walking the parsed syntax tree bottom-up, replacing each custom component with its equivalent plain-text representation. It handles dozens of custom components (like AlertBox, Snippet, Terminal) by applying context-specific rules, while unknown components are gracefully unwrapped so their content survives the export. The result is a self-contained Markdown file that's readable by humans and LLMs without any interactive elements.

explanations.30: This pulls the `unified` export directly (not `.default`) because the `unified` package exports it as a named export, unlike most of the remark plugins.
explanations.45: This imports remark-parse but accesses `.default` because it's an ESM package being loaded via CommonJS require(); the `.default` property exposes the actual parser function.
explanations.128: The regex strips away annotations like " (staged diff)" that authors add to filenames — anything in parentheses at the end — so `path.extname()` works correctly on just the actual filename.
explanations.170: Template literals like `` `\nfoo\n` `` can be safely evaluated at build time only if they have no `${...}` interpolations; static ones are unwrapped by concatenating their string parts.
explanations.212: This checks if the object is a `require()` result by looking for the `__requirePath` marker set earlier in the `CallExpression` case, preserving the path even through property access like `.default`.
explanations.270: MDX stores JSX expression attribute values as an estree (JavaScript abstract syntax tree) nested inside `data.estree.body[0]`, so this unpacks it to find the actual expression node.
explanations.296: When given an array of mdast nodes (like a list of paragraphs), join them with newlines; when given individual nodes, their internal children concatenate directly without separation.
explanations.338: This creates a minimal parser that only understands inline Markdown syntax (bold, code, links within a paragraph) — not block-level elements — for parsing strings like AlertBox titles that embed formatting.
explanations.343: After parsing the string as full Markdown, extract only the `paragraph` nodes because top-level paragraphs are where inline content lives; discard any block-level structures that don't apply here.
explanations.397: The `strongParsed` function expects strings that may contain Markdown syntax, so this parses the title string into real inline nodes rather than wrapping it as a literal.
explanations.406: Wrap the value in an `inlineCode` node (which becomes `` `value` `` in Markdown) instead of plain text because this is table cell content that needs consistent formatting.
explanations.438: If the component has a `source` attribute pointing to an external file, read that file; otherwise, use the inline `code` attribute; otherwise, extract text from the component's children.
explanations.519: Only add the install command block if the `install` attribute exists; combine the command and its output (if provided) into a single code block for readability.
explanations.553: The `variant` attribute determines if this is an ordered list (most steps) or an unordered list (the `remember` variant uses bullets instead).
explanations.571: Convert each shortcut's key array like `['Ctrl', 'K']` into display nodes like `[Ctrl]+[K]`, and each description from JSX/string into plain text.
explanations.649: The `file` attribute contains a `__requirePath` marker (set by `literalFromEstree` when it encounters a `require()` call) — extract the path since the final hashed build URL is unknowable at export time.
explanations.682: Headings cannot contain block-level children (like nested paragraphs), so unwrap any paragraphs into their inline children to avoid malformed mdast.
explanations.695: Only absolute paths (`/img/x`) and full HTTP(S) URLs survive the export as working image links; relative paths from `require()` get fingerprinted by webpack into hashes this script can't predict.
explanations.708: A step can be a plain string or an object with `content`/`substeps` properties; normalize both into the object shape so the next section handles them uniformly.
explanations.748: Insert a `+` separator before each key except the first one, so `['Ctrl', 'K']` becomes `Ctrl+K` (not `+Ctrl+K`).
explanations.766: Convert the component's name to lowercase for comparison since both `<Div>` and `<div>` are valid JSX and should be treated the same way.
explanations.819: Recursively transform the node's children first (bottom-up) before checking the node's own type, so nested components are already degraded before the parent sees them.
explanations.826: A bare `{expression}` in the source (not inside an attribute) — convert it to a text node if it's non-empty, otherwise drop it, since most expressions in this corpus are inside code fences anyway.
explanations.857: For inline directives that aren't real `:::` directives (like `user_id:group_id`), reconstruct the original text from the raw source using character offsets to avoid losing the word.
explanations.897: HTML tags are always lowercase in the component name (because the JSX parser lowercases them), while custom React components start with uppercase — use this to distinguish them.
explanations.950: If the admonitions plugin is available, pre-process the source to convert Docasaurus's shorthand `:::tip Free text` into the remark-directive format `:::tip[Free text]` that the plugin expects.
explanations.956: The directive transformer is a separate processor that only applies Docasaurus's internal admonition metadata logic; run it as a second pass after parsing so it annotates the tree with type/title info.
